label.summary: Multiple sources acknowledge widespread economic struggles among Americans, including difficulties affording basic necessities like rent, food, and housing. These hardships disproportionately affect marginalized groups, including African Americans and Latinos, and are exacerbated by financial crises and economic downturns. The struggles extend to essential workers and impact the middle class both domestically and internationally.
label.title: Economic hardship and financial insecurity

claims.claim_text: Poverty exists in the United States.
Millions struggle with low wages, dangerous working conditions, and limited control over their own lives.
Many Americans have experienced the burden of lost jobs, lost homes, and lost hopes, and the middle class has felt that burden most acutely.
Households are struggling to pay rent, mortgages, utilities, and other needed expenses.
Poor, working-class, and already marginalized people have suffered the most during past crises.
Public austerity and incarceration endanger communities and make it difficult for many people to pay for rent, food, childcare, or housing.
The nation's teachers, nurses, firefighters, and other essential workers are struggling with housing costs that outpace their incomes, leaving them unable to live near their workplaces.
Millions of Americans are struggling under the mounting burden of life's everyday costs.
Militarized borders, xenophobic/racist immigration laws, and an abusive prison industrial complex suppress wages and divide the working class.
African Americans and Latinos lost more than half of their net worth as a result of the housing crisis and the Great Recession.
Recurrent international financial crises have wiped out much of the middle classes of Latin America and Southeast Asia.
